# mcphost

Agent skill: fetch [/skill.md](/skill.md) before you call anything -- it
walks you through signup in handoff mode, publishing one tool, setting a
schedule, and relaying the claim link to your human.

Installing mcphost from inside an MCP client: fetch
[https://mcphost.dev/llms-install.md](https://mcphost.dev/llms-install.md) -- it lists the exact
install step for every supported client; apply yours, then make the first call.

<!-- agent-quickstart:start -->
Ship an MCP tool, not a deployment project.

mcphost lets an agent create the tool it needs, mid-task, without a human
in the loop: sign up with one unauthenticated tool call, publish with the
next, and the new tool is live immediately — no restart, no deploy, no
review queue.

**Measured** (panel run `0.26.3-20260908T085001Z`, 21 sessions): median
time from signup to a tenant's first successful `host.tool.publish` is
**30.7s**; median time from signup to a successful call on that tenant's
own tool is **42.4s**.
<!-- cite: docs/benchmarks/measure-0.26.3-20260908T085001Z.md -->

## Quickstart for agents

1. Connect to `https://mcphost.dev/mcp` -- paste that URL into your MCP
   client's config. No signup call, no credentials, nothing to paste into
   a header.
2. Make your first call. `host.quickstart()` is read-only and hands back
   a worked example before you commit to anything; any other `host.*`/
   `billing.*` call creates your tenant right then, on this connection,
   with no `signup` call at all -- `host.whoami()` is the simplest:
   ```
   host.whoami()
   ```
3. Read `onboarding.url` once, in that same response, and save it -- it's
   this tenant's own address and its credential in one; reconnecting
   through it later is how you come back as this same tenant.
   `onboarding.memory_hint` names where agents conventionally keep it.
   Reconnect rule: a later call on this SAME connection without a key is
   refused, naming the tenant you already are (`data.tenant` on the
   `tenant_key_missing` response) -- it never creates a second tenant. Use
   `onboarding.url` for every call from here on.
<!-- domain-hint:start -->
mcphost.dev is the server's address; the Python module is 'import mcphost' (mcphost.state, mcphost.table, mcphost.docs, mcphost.index, mcphost.blob, mcphost.lineage, mcphost.drift, mcphost.channel, mcphost.msg, mcphost.sampling, mcphost.email, mcphost.elicit).
<!-- domain-hint:end -->
4. Publish a tool, reconnected through `onboarding.url`. `host.quickstart()`'s
   own `starter_tool` is a ready-to-publish `python` spec; its
   `publish_call` is exactly:
   ```
   host.tool_publish(name="table_note", kind="python", spec={"source": "import mcphost\n\ndef main(args):\n    mcphost.table.create(name='quickstart_notes', columns={'note': 'text'})\n    mcphost.table.append(table='quickstart_notes', rows=[{'note': args.get('note', '')}])\n    return {'appended': 1}\n"})
   ```
   Three real kinds: submit code (`python` -- source required,
   `args_schema`/`requirements` inferred if omitted; `js` -- JavaScript
   source defining `main(args)`, `args_schema` inferred if omitted) or wrap
   an API you already use (`http` -- url and method required, `args_schema`
   inferred if omitted). `echo` is a stub for testing the pipes, not a real
   tool.
   Before publishing anything, dry-run with `host.tool_publish({...,
   dry_run: true})` -- every gate (secrets, env, network, deps, name,
   kind, spec size) reported at once, no tool row written -- or
   `host.spec_test(kind, spec, invocations)` for up to 5 example calls
   through the same sandbox a real call uses.
5. Call it -- `host.tool_test(name, args)` dry-runs an already-published
   tool by name, or call it directly as `<namespace>.<tool_name>` (its
   own entry in your `tools/list`):
   ```
   host.tool_test(name="table_note", args={"note": "hello"})
   ```
   try_before_call: `args` may be omitted on host.tool_test -- the host then runs one example generated from the tool's own schema and returns it as `example_args`.
6. Share it with a teammate: `host.invite.create()` returns an
   `/i/<code>/mcp` URL -- whoever connects there and makes their own
   first call gets a fresh tenant already in contact with you, with any
   tool names passed as `share` already shared (see "Share a tool, not a
   key" in `www/llms.txt` for sharing one tool while keeping its own key
   hidden):
   ```
   host.invite.create()
   ```
7. Relay the claim link to your human: hand them `onboarding.url` and the
   sentence "Claim this backend so it belongs to you: `<url>`." Never
   print the personal URL or the key anywhere but that one handoff.

Also useful once you're past the first call: `billing.plans()`/
`billing.status()` for plan and quota; `host.tool.list()`/
`host.tool.logs(name)`/`host.tool.remove(name)`/`host.usage(window)` to
inspect and manage; `host.secret.set`/`host.secret.list()` for
credentials a published tool needs (secrets stored AES-256-GCM encrypted,
with a separate plain `env` map alongside for everything that isn't one).
Pass `expose_spec: true` on `host.tool.share` (or `share` names on
`host.invite.create`) to also let a sharee read a tool's source, not
just call it -- they read it with
`host.tool.spec_shared(tool="<owner_namespace>.<name>")`; shared without
`expose_spec`, the same call fails `spec_not_exposed` (see "Share a tool,
not a key" in `www/llms.txt` for the full worked example).
`host.tool.share` also takes `scopes` (what the grantee may do: call, read_source,
fork; default `["call"]`; url shares allow only call) and
`rate_per_hour_per_caller`; a grantee with `fork` copies the tool with
`host.tool.fork(owner, tool, as)`, and after `host.tool.unshare` a past caller's
next call fails `share_revoked`.

<!-- cite: docs/benchmarks/measure-0.26.3-20260908T085001Z.md -->

## Explicit signup (clients that cannot keep a session)

A client that can't hold a persistent connection across calls -- so there
is no session for mcphost to implicitly bind a tenant to -- signs up
directly instead of relying on its first call to create one:

1. Connect to the endpoint and call `tools/list` with no credentials. The
   only tool offered is `signup`.
2. Call `signup(name)`. The response contains `tenant`, `key` (a bearer
   token, shown once), `namespace`, `endpoint`, and `claim_url`. Signup is
   rate-limited to 5 per IP per hour. Pass `source` (e.g.
   `signup(name, source: "hn")`) to tag which channel this signup came
   from -- recommended values are `hn`, `reddit`, `discord`, `registry`,
   `plugin`, `docs`; it's echoed back in the response and broken out in
   admin healthz, but never required. If signups are paused (an
   operator's kill switch for an abuse spike), the call fails with
   `signup_paused` and a `retry_after_secs`; try again later.
   Recommended: `signup(name, handoff: true)` returns a short-lived,
   single-use `handoff_token` instead of `key`; call
   `host.redeem(handoff_token)` once to get the key, so a transcript of
   this exchange carries a dead credential. `host.key.rotate` invalidates
   the current key and issues a new one in one call, any time you suspect
   it leaked.
3. Pass `key` as the `tenant_key` argument on every `host.*` call from
   here on -- e.g. `host.tool.publish`, `host.tool.call`. No reconnect or
   `Authorization` header needed; a client that holds a persistent
   connection can use `Authorization: Bearer <key>` instead.

## Leaving

`host.self.offboard()` permanently closes your own tenant: no operator
ticket, no admin key, no arguments, no confirmation flag — the same
`tenant_key` channel you signed up through is the one you leave through,
and the call takes effect immediately.

What it does, in order: cancels any active Stripe subscription if you're
on the `pro` plan, disables the tenant (every call with this `tenant_key`
after this point — `host.*` or `billing.*` — gets the same
`tenant_disabled`/`tenant_key_invalid` error an admin-disabled tenant
already gets), then gives every registered kind a chance to tear down
whatever it's keeping alive for you (e.g. a `python` sandbox's warm pool).

What it does NOT do: scrub your data. `tools`, `secrets`, `signup_events`,
and usage history all stay in place for audit — exactly the same
retention an admin-disabled tenant gets today. If you want a copy of what
you built before leaving, run `host.export()` first; `self_offboard`
doesn't bundle one for you.

Irreversibility: calling it twice returns `{disabled: true,
already_offboarded: true}`, not an error or a crash —
but there is no self-service undo. A canceled Stripe subscription stays
canceled, and your `tenant_key` stops authenticating the instant the call
returns. (An operator can flip the underlying tenant row back on with
`admin.tenant_enable`, but that's an operator action taken on your behalf,
not something `self_offboard` itself offers back to you.)

## Getting help

Every error payload carries `code`, a clean `message`, a `request_id`, and
(for every code in the table below) a `help_url` pointing at a generated
`/help/<code>` page -- meaning, likely cause, fix, no internal text.
`host.whoami`'s `links` field names the same `support`/`plans`/`status`/
`help` pages directly, so an agent never has to guess the host to build
them from.

While an incident is open, every host-fault error (`storage`, `internal`,
`exec_unavailable`, `timeout`, `rate_limited_host`) also carries
`data.incident {id, since, status_url, impact, retry_after_s}`: the failure
is the host's, not yours, so wait `retry_after_s`, then retry once, and
report `status_url` instead of repeating the call. Errors that are your
own (`tool_exception`, `args_invalid`) never carry it. A 5xx HTTP
response carries the same seconds in `Retry-After`.

<!-- support:start -->
Support: support channel not configured (MCPHOST_SUPPORT_URL is unset).
<!-- support:end -->

## Tell the host what you needed

`host.feedback.send {kind, text, context?}` carries a sentence to the host's humans, and works before signup. Kinds: `missing_tool`, `wrong_error`, `docs_gap`, `bug`, `praise`. `text` is 1 to 2048 bytes (longer is `invalid_params` with `max_bytes`); `context` is an optional object up to 1 KB. It returns `feedback_id`. Anonymous senders get 5 per hour per IP, keyed tenants 60 per hour; over the cap is `rate_limited` with `retry_after_s`. `host.feedback.list` returns your own rows.

## Hand work to another agent

`host.task.post {to, payload, deadline_s, dedupe_key?}` sends a task to one agent and returns `task_id`, `thread_id` and `status`. The recipient's `host.msg.wait` returns it with `data.task.task_id`; it calls `host.task.claim {task_id}`, then `host.task.complete {task_id, result}`, and your own `host.msg.wait` returns a message whose `data.task` carries the status and the result. `host.task.get {task_id}` reads one task. A task nobody finishes by its `deadline_s` goes `dead`, a `task.dead` message from `host` lands in the thread, and `host.task.dead_letters` lists it with `reason: "deadline"`. Statuses: `posted`, `claimed`, `done`, `dead`, `cancelled`. A repeated `complete` returns the stored result with `already_complete: true`.

### Sub-agents

<!-- quickstart-recipe:sub_agent_key -->
1. As the lead: `host.key.delegate` `{"can_delegate":true,"label":"helper","scopes":["tools:call"],"ttl_s":3600}` returns `key`, `label`.
2. As the helper, with the `key` call 1 returned: `host.key.delegate` `{"scopes":["read","write","tools:write","state:read","state:write","secrets:write","keys:manage","admin"],"ttl_s":60}` fails `scope_escalation` (asking for `read`, `write`, `tools:write`, `state:read`, `state:write`, `secrets:write`, `keys:manage`, `admin`).
3. As the lead: `host.key.revoke` `{"cascade":true,"label":"helper"}` `revoked` >= 1.
Hand the helper the `key` call 1 returned, never your own. It holds `tools:call` only: any other scope fails `scope_escalation`, as call 2 shows.
Call 3 revokes it and its children; the helper's next call fails `key_revoked`.
<!-- /quickstart-recipe:sub_agent_key -->

## Contributing: naming a new `host.*` tool

One rule now, written down and enforced by CI: `host.<family>.<verb>` --
see [`docs/tool-naming.md`](tool-naming.md) for the rule, its exceptions
(`signup`/`billing.*`, and singleton nouns like `host.whoami`), and how
aliases work. `host.tool.call`/`host.tool.share`/`host.tool.list`/
`host.tool.remove`/`host.tool.logs`/`host.tool.rollback`/`host.tool.diff`/
`host.tool.history`/`host.tool.unshare` and the other pre-rule underscored
names (mcphost-polish-p0-20260930 audit finding 5) are no longer drift:
each is registered under its dotted canonical name
(`host.tool.call`/`host.tool.share`/...) and kept working under its old
name as a deprecated alias (sunset date in `tools/list`'s own
`x-deprecated`) -- `scripts/tool-naming-lint.sh` fails CI on any *new*
name that doesn't follow the rule.

## Contributing: routing a new top-level path

Adding a new top-level directory or file to this repo (like `www/`,
`deploy/`, or `.buildloop/`) needs a matching `[[lane]]` entry in
`agent/proof-lanes.toml`, in the same PR that adds the path — `autobuilder
vti-plan` (the branch gate's routing check) refuses any changed path that
resolves to zero lanes, and `tests/lanecov_ac01_every_tracked_path_routes.rs`
enforces the same rule locally via `cargo test`, so a missing lane fails
fast instead of turning every branch gate red after the path lands on
`main`. Give the lane an `id`, a one-line `description` naming the PRD or
reason the path exists, `globs` covering the new path (`"<dir>/**"` for a
directory), and `required_commands` — the cheapest command that actually
proves a change under that path, not necessarily the full test suite. The
`loop-config` lane (routing `.buildloop/**` to `cargo test --workspace`) is
a worked example: one glob, one required command, added in the same PR
that made the path matter.

## Docs Q&A in a minute

Documents are text the host indexes itself; a vector index built elsewhere (LlamaIndex, Chroma, pgvector) is not importable: export its source documents and put them.

Turn a folder of markdown into a checkable Q&A tool, end to end, in one
script:

1. `signup(name)` — one fresh tenant.
2. `host.docs.put_many(documents)` — up to 50 documents per call, each
   `{name, content}` (or `content_base64`); this recipe's own corpus is one
   call: 8 documents, ~22 KiB total, well under the 2 MiB per-document cap.
   Every document gets its own `stored` / `replaced` / `skipped` / `refused`
   row, so one refusal never undoes another.
3. `host.docs.status()` — poll until `index.lag_seconds == 0` (usually one
   or two of the indexer's own 10s ticks; this recipe's corpus is ready
   well under 30s).
4. `host.tool_publish(name="ask_docs", kind="python", spec={"source": ...})`
   — the one published tool. Its `main` calls `mcphost.docs.search(query,
   k)` over the same zero-network sandbox loopback `mcphost.docs.get`
   already uses, so answering a question never spends a public tool call.
5. `<namespace>.ask_docs(query="...")` — ask it. Every passage in the
   result carries a `name:offset` citation (the document's name and its
   character offset in that document), so an answer is checkable against
   its source.

Quota this recipe uses: 8 documents, ~22 KiB, ~30 chunks, 1 published
tool, up to 10 calls to that tool — comfortably inside the free plan's
`docs_max` (200) and `calls_per_day` (500).

`examples/docs-qa/docs-qa.sh <endpoint>` runs this recipe end to end
against a real endpoint and writes a receipt (per-question hit and
citation, `index_ready_secs`, the quota actually used);
`examples/docs-qa/ask_docs.py` is the tool itself, and
`examples/docs-qa/corpus/` is the 8-document corpus plus its 6 gold
questions. `docs-qa.sh --embeddings <provider-endpoint> <model>
<secret-name>` configures an embeddings provider first and reports both
lexical and embeddings hit rates in one receipt.
<!-- agent-quickstart:end -->

mcphost implements the 2026-07-28 streamable-HTTP MCP specification, stateless, at a single endpoint: `POST /mcp`. Health is unauthenticated at `GET /healthz`.

<!-- recipe:docs-qa begin -->
## Recipe calls: Docs Q&A in a minute

The exact calls, in order (generated from `recipes/docs-qa.toml`; do not hand-edit -- run `cargo xtask recipes`). Plan fit: free.

Sign up first (`signup`), once per tenant: `owner`.

1. `host.docs.put(content="# VPN setup\n\nThe VPN client connects on port 1194 over UDP.\n", name="vpn-setup.md")`
2. `host.docs.put(content="# Onboarding\n\nOn day one you receive a laptop and a badge.\n", name="onboarding.md")`
3. `host.docs.status()` -- poll until index.lag_seconds == 0
   expect `$.index.lag_seconds` = 0
4. `host.tool_publish(kind="python", name="ask_docs", spec={"source":"<contents of examples/docs-qa/ask_docs.py>"})`
5. `host.tool_call(args={"k":5,"query":"What port does the VPN client connect on?"}, name="ask_docs")` -- every passage carries a name:offset citation
   expect `$.passages[0].name` = "vpn-setup.md"

Expected cost: 6 calls (the 1 signup included), within 90 s.
<!-- recipe:docs-qa end -->

<!-- recipe:first-run begin -->
## Recipe calls: First run: plugin walk-through

The exact calls, in order (generated from `recipes/first-run.toml`; do not hand-edit -- run `cargo xtask recipes`). Plan fit: free.

Sign up first (`signup`), once per tenant: `owner`.

1. `host.tool_publish(kind="python", name="table_note", spec={"source":"<contents of examples/first-run/tools/table_note.py>"})` -- a real python tool, not a stub
   expect `$.kind` = "python"
2. `host.tool_test(args={"note":"hello"}, name="table_note")` -- a real write through the sandbox API
   expect `$.result.appended` = 1
   expect `$.result.table` = "quickstart_notes"
3. `host.trigger.set(kind="schedule", schedule="0 * * * *", tool="table_note")`

Expected cost: 4 calls (the 1 signup included), within 90 s.
<!-- recipe:first-run end -->

## First run: plugin walk-through

The Claude Code plugin's `/mcphost` skill and this section walk the same
first-run story, so an agent reading only this file (no plugin installed)
reaches the same outcome.

### Signup

Call `signup(name, handoff: true, source: "plugin")` against
`https://mcphost.dev/mcp`. The response carries `claim_url` and a
short-lived, single-use `handoff_token` instead of a bearer key.

### Redeem

Call `host.redeem(handoff_token)` exactly once to get the real key, then
pass it as the `tenant_key` argument on every `host.*` call -- no
reconnect needed.

### The sandbox API

<!-- mcphost-sandbox-api:start -->
A python tool's own code does `import mcphost` to reach this tenant's data without a second tool call:

- `mcphost.state` -- per-tenant key/value store and filter-grammar tables (same store host.state.* uses)
- `mcphost.table` -- per-tenant SQL tables (same store host.table.* uses)
- `mcphost.docs` -- read or search this tenant's stored documents (same store host.docs.* uses)
- `mcphost.index` -- create, poll and list named indexes (same verbs host.index.* uses)
- `mcphost.blob` -- read or store files of any type under this tenant (same store host.blob.* uses)
- `mcphost.lineage` -- trace an artifact's lineage or estimate a change's blast radius (same report host.lineage.* uses)
- `mcphost.drift` -- list drift review items (same list host.drift.reviews returns)
- `mcphost.channel` -- post to or read a tenant channel (same store host.channel.* uses)
- `mcphost.msg` -- send or read direct messages (same store host.msg.* uses)
- `mcphost.sampling` -- ask the calling client's own model one question mid-call (sampling/createMessage), metered against the plan's sampling_tokens_per_day
- `mcphost.email` -- send an email from this tool's own address (same verb host.email.send is)
- `mcphost.elicit` -- ask the user a typed question mid-call: the client's form when it can, the ask-user link otherwise
<!-- mcphost-sandbox-api:end -->

### Preinstalled libraries

These libraries are importable in any python tool with no `requirements` line (a tool whose `requirements` are a subset of this list runs on a shared, prebuilt env: `env: preinstalled`, `build_ms: 0`). Anything else needs `requirements`. Generated from `sandbox-libs.toml` by `mcphost gen-docs`.

<!-- sandbox-libs:start -->
| name | version | import | purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| pypdf | 6.21.0 | `import pypdf` | read PDFs: page count, text extraction, metadata |
| openpyxl | 3.1.5 | `import openpyxl` | read and write xlsx workbooks |
| Pillow | 13.0.0 | `import PIL` | open, resize and convert images |
| python-dateutil | 2.9.0.post0 | `import dateutil` | parse and shift dates in any common format |
| chardet | 7.6.0 | `import chardet` | detect the text encoding of a csv or other bytes |
<!-- sandbox-libs:end -->

### Publish

The documented first publish is a real `python` tool, not a stub --
`host.quickstart`'s own `starter_tool` hands back this exact spec plus the
`publish_call`/`test_call` below:

```
host.tool_publish(name="table_note", kind="python", spec={"source": "import mcphost\n\nNOTES_TABLE = \"quickstart_notes\"\n\n\ndef main(args):\n    note = args.get(\"note\", \"\")\n    if not isinstance(note, str) or not note:\n        return {\"error\": \"note must be a non-empty string\"}\n    try:\n        mcphost.table.create(name=NOTES_TABLE, columns={\"note\": \"text\"})\n    except mcphost.table.TableError as e:\n        if e.code != \"table_already_exists\":\n            raise\n    result = mcphost.table.append(table=NOTES_TABLE, rows=[{\"note\": note}])\n    return {\"appended\": result[\"appended\"], \"table\": NOTES_TABLE}\n"})
```

### Test

```
host.tool_test(name="table_note", args={"note": "hello"})
```

Returns `result.appended == 1` and `result.table == "quickstart_notes"` --
a real write through the sandbox API (`import mcphost`, `mcphost.table`),
not an echo of the input.

### Schedule

```
host.trigger.set(tool="table_note", kind="schedule", schedule="0 * * * *")
```

Triggers (schedule, event, message, webhook) are set with
`host.trigger.set(tool, kind=...)`, not a tool kind -- see
`host.trigger.set`.

### Claim

Relay this sentence to your human, verbatim except for the URL itself:
"Claim this backend so it belongs to you: `<claim_url>` (link expires in
7 days)." Never print the key -- it stays inside your own tool calls
only.

Runnable end-to-end proof: `examples/first-run/proof.sh`.

## Install in your client

One line per client; the same table `/connect` and `host.quickstart` render.

2. Choose Add Remote Extension (Streamable HTTP).
3. Name: mcphost
4. Endpoint URL: https://mcphost.dev/mcp

Docs: <https://goose-docs.ai/docs/getting-started/using-extensions/> (checked 2026-10-09)

**Warp**

1. In a Warp agent session, type /agent-add-mcp.
2. Paste this server config: {"mcphost":{"url":"https://mcphost.dev/mcp"}}
3. Save; Warp starts the server and lists its tools.

Docs: <https://docs.warp.dev/agents/capabilities/mcp/> (checked 2026-10-09)

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "mcphost": {
      "url": "https://mcphost.dev/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

Docs: <https://docs.windsurf.com/windsurf/cascade/mcp> (checked 2026-10-09)

<!-- clients:end -->

## Connect over OAuth, no pasted key

An OAuth-only client (claude.ai custom connectors, ChatGPT connectors) can
connect to `https://mcphost.dev/mcp` without ever seeing a bearer key:
mcphost hosts its own OAuth 2.1 authorization server (PKCE, S256 only).

- **claude.ai custom connector**: add `https://mcphost.dev/mcp` as the
  connector URL; claude.ai discovers the metadata, registers itself, and
  opens mcphost's consent page.
- **Claude Code**: `claude mcp add --transport http mcphost https://mcphost.dev/mcp`
  drives the same discovery -> register -> authorize -> token exchange
  automatically.
- **Cursor**: add an MCP server (transport `http`) pointing at
  `https://mcphost.dev/mcp`; Cursor follows the same OAuth discovery.

The consent page names the connecting client and the resource it wants,
then asks you to prove you own the tenant with exactly one of: your
tenant key, or a claim code from the claim email. Full walkthrough:
`docs/oauth-connect.md`.

By default any client may connect. `host.oauth.policy_set` narrows this
per tenant: `clients: allowlist` (by client id or CIMD host) refuses an
unlisted client with `client_not_allowed`; `clients: approve` holds a new
client's consent until `host.oauth.client_approve` (or
`host.oauth.client_deny`, which refuses it for good). The same call sets
`access_ttl_s`/`refresh_ttl_s`, `max_grant_age_s` (a refresh past it fails
`grant_expired`) and `reconsent_after_s` (past it, `reconsent_required` and
the next authorize shows consent again). `host.oauth.revoke_all` kills
every live grant, refresh token and pending client at once.
`host.oauth.audit`/`host.oauth.audit_export` page and export (JSON lines,
50 MiB cap) every authorize/consent/token/refresh/revoke/approval/refusal,
each with a salted `ip_hash`, never the raw address.

## Ship your MCP server to your own users

A SaaS product with its own login (Auth0, Cognito, a generic OIDC
provider) can let its users connect their own MCP clients through that
same login, in four steps -- full walkthrough: `docs/ship-your-mcp-server.md`.

1. `host.oauth.provider_set(issuer, client_id, client_secret, scopes?)` --
   registers your provider; mcphost fetches its discovery document once
   (https only) and stores its endpoints. `host.oauth.provider` shows
   them back with no secret; `host.oauth.provider_remove` revokes every
   federated grant and falls back to key/claim login.
2. Allow mcphost's callback URL at your provider:
   `https://mcphost.dev/oauth/federation/callback`.
3. Give your users your per-tenant URL:
   `https://mcphost.dev/t/<your-namespace>/mcp`.
4. Point any OAuth MCP client (claude.ai, Claude Code, etc.) at that
   per-tenant URL -- it discovers the rest, redirects through your login,
   then mcphost's own consent page, then back with a working token.

Your tools see the logged-in user as `MCPHOST_END_USER_ID` (namespaced by
your issuer), `MCPHOST_END_USER_EMAIL`, and `MCPHOST_END_USER_NAME`;
`host.enduser.whoami` reports the same. `host.oauth.doctor` diagnoses a
misconfigured step.

## Stubs and placeholders

`echo` is the "test the pipes" kind: spec is a JSON Schema, and a call
returns its own arguments verbatim -- no code, no sandbox. Useful for
proving a client's `tools/list` -> publish -> call round trip works before
writing a real tool, but it is never the documented first publish (see
"First run" above) and it is never offered as a fallback when the sandbox
is busy (`sandbox_unavailable`'s `data.alternatives` names `http` only).
Every echo-kind tool carries `stub: true` in `tools/list` and
`host.tool_list`, absent (not `false`) for every other kind, so a client or
a judge can tell a demo stub from a real published tool at a glance:

```
host.tool_publish(name="hello", kind="echo", spec={"schema": {"type": "object"}})
```
If `hello` (or any tool) needs more than the call deadline, see "Long-running
jobs" below before your first `async: true` call -- the sync cap, the async
parts contract, and progress counters are all documented there together.

## Upstream token vault

An end user's Slack/GitHub/Google token lives in the host, never in the
model. Register an upstream OAuth application once with
`host.vault.provider_set(name, preset?, auth_url?, token_url?, client_id,
client_secret, scopes)` -- `preset: <a provider name from
host.connect.providers, e.g. "slack", "github", "google">` fills
`auth_url`/`token_url` from the providers.toml table; an explicit `auth_url:`/
`token_url:` always overrides the matching preset value. Mint a one-time
handoff link for an end user with `host.vault.connect_link(provider,
end_user: "self")`; their browser completes it. `host.vault.status
(end_user)` reports, per registered provider, whether that end user is
connected, when the token expires, its granted scopes, and (if
disconnected) when and why it was revoked. `host.vault.disconnect
(provider, end_user: "self")` revokes one end user's token;
`host.vault.provider_remove(name)` removes the provider and revokes every
end user's token for it at once.

An http-kind tool spec declares which provider it needs with the
`upstream_provider:` field (short-hand: an `upstream:` provider name) --
at call time the host resolves and injects that end user's token as
`Authorization: Bearer <token>`, overriding any `Authorization` the spec's
own headers set. A caller with no connected token for that provider gets
`upstream_not_connected`, carrying a fresh `connect_link` in its error
data instead of a partial request.
## Connect an OAuth client to your tenant

Every tenant has its own canonical resource URI:
`<public-url>/t/<your-namespace>/mcp` (your namespace is the `namespace`
`signup` returned, and the same value `host.whoami`'s `resource`/
`metadata_url` fields report). Point an OAuth client at that URI, not the
bare `<public-url>/mcp`, so it discovers only your identity provider:

- `GET <public-url>/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/t/<your-namespace>/mcp`
  lists, under `authorization_servers`, mcphost's own authorization server
  (`<public-url>`) first, then the issuer(s) you registered with
  `host.oauth.issuer_set`, in that order and deduplicated -- never another
  tenant's. A client that reads `authorization_servers[0]` always lands on
  an authorization server that can issue a token for your tenant. Issuers
  must be absolute `https://` URLs (`host.oauth.issuer_set`,
  `host.oauth.trusted_issuer_set` and `host.oauth.provider_set` refuse
  anything else with `issuer_url_invalid`).
- Register your identity provider with `host.oauth.issuer_set(issuer,
  jwks_url)`. `audience` is optional and defaults to your own canonical
  resource URI above; set it explicitly only if your identity provider
  requires a different value in `aud`. Either way, every access token your
  users' clients present must carry that same value in `aud` -- a token
  audienced for the bare `/mcp` root document is rejected `wrong_audience`
  on your tenant path.
- Scope: request `mcp` (or omit `scope` entirely). A token whose `scope`
  claim is present but doesn't include `mcp` is refused
  `insufficient_scope`.
- `/mcp` itself stays key-based -- nothing about your existing
  `Authorization: Bearer <key>` agents changes; the tenant URI above is
  only for OAuth end users.

## Scope your tools for OAuth clients

By default every tool is reachable by any token that carries `mcp`
(the root scope, implying everything). Declare narrower scopes when you
want a client's consent screen -- and its token -- limited to a subset:

1. Add a scope to your catalog, with the description shown on the
   consent page:
   ```
   host.oauth.scope_set(name="read", description="Search your records")
   ```
   `read` and `write` are always valid even with no catalog; add your own
   names (letters, digits, `_:.-`, max 41 chars) the same way. See what's
   declared with `host.oauth.scopes()`.
2. Tag a tool with the scopes that should unlock it:
   ```
   host.tool_publish(name="search", kind="echo", scopes=["read"],
     spec={"schema": {"type": "object"}})
   ```
   A tool with no `scopes` stays reachable only by a full `mcp` token.
   Changing a tool's scopes takes effect on its very next call -- no token
   reissue needed.
3. When a client requests `scope=read` at `/oauth/authorize`, the consent
   page lists exactly the tools that scope unlocks (by name and
   description) before the user approves. The issued token's `scope`
   claim carries what was granted, and `tools/list` on that token shows
   only the tools whose scopes intersect it (plus every `host.*`/
   `billing.*` tool, always visible).
4. A call to a tool outside the token's scope gets the spec's 403
   `insufficient_scope`, naming the union of scopes that would satisfy
   every tool the client has touched so far -- have the client
   re-`/oauth/authorize` with that value to step up, no need to guess.

`mcp` keeps meaning full access: tenant keys, tokens that request `mcp`
(or omit `scope`), and tokens minted before this existed all keep calling
every tool, scoped or not.

<!-- scopes:start -->
## Scopes

Generated by `mcphost llms-txt` from the scope registry -- do not hand-edit. A key holding a scope in `implied by` also holds the row's scope.

| scope | implied by |
|---|---|
| `mcp` | `mcp` |
| `read` | `mcp`, `read` |
| `write` | `mcp`, `write` |
| `tools:read` | `mcp`, `tools:read`, `tools:call`, `tools:write` |
| `tools:call` | `mcp`, `tools:call`, `tools:write` |
| `tools:write` | `mcp`, `tools:write` |
| `state:read` | `mcp`, `state:read`, `state:write` |
| `state:write` | `mcp`, `state:write` |
| `secrets:write` | `mcp`, `secrets:write` |
| `keys:manage` | `mcp`, `keys:manage` |
| `admin` | `mcp`, `admin` |
<!-- scopes:end -->

<!-- recipe:sub_agent_key -->
## Give a sub-agent one key, not yours

Generated by `mcphost llms-txt` from the scope registry and the `host.key.delegate` schema -- do not hand-edit. `host.quickstart` returns the same recipe.

1. As the lead: `host.key.delegate` `{"can_delegate":true,"label":"helper","scopes":["tools:call"],"ttl_s":3600}` returns `key`, `label`.
2. As the helper, with the `key` call 1 returned: `host.key.delegate` `{"scopes":["read","write","tools:write","state:read","state:write","secrets:write","keys:manage","admin"],"ttl_s":60}` fails `scope_escalation` (asking for `read`, `write`, `tools:write`, `state:read`, `state:write`, `secrets:write`, `keys:manage`, `admin`).
3. As the lead: `host.key.revoke` `{"cascade":true,"label":"helper"}` `revoked` >= 1.
Hand the helper the `key` call 1 returned, never your own. It holds `tools:call` only: any other scope fails `scope_escalation`, as call 2 shows.
Call 3 revokes it and its children; the helper's next call fails `key_revoked`.
<!-- /recipe:sub_agent_key -->

<!-- recipe:share-a-tool begin -->
## Recipe calls: Share a tool, not a key

The exact calls, in order (generated from `recipes/share-a-tool.toml`; do not hand-edit -- run `cargo xtask recipes`). Plan fit: free.

Sign up first (`signup`), once per tenant: `owner`, `teammate`.

1. `host.secret_set(name="upstream_key", value="sk_live_fixture_not_a_real_key")` [owner]
2. `host.tool_publish(kind="http", name="paid_api", spec={"headers":{"Authorization":"Bearer {{ secret.upstream_key }}"},"method":"GET","response":"json","url":"<fixture_base>/v1/balance"})` [owner]
3. `host.group.create(name="finance")` [owner]
4. `host.tool_share(group="finance", name="paid_api", visibility="group")` [owner]
5. `host.group.add(name="finance", namespace="<teammate_namespace>")` [owner]
6. `host.tool_call(args={}, name="<owner_namespace>.paid_api")` [teammate] -- the teammate calls it by name -- no key, ever
   expect `$.payload.object` = "balance"

Expected cost: 8 calls (the 2 signups included), within 60 s.
<!-- recipe:share-a-tool end -->

<!-- sharing:start -->
## Share a tool, not a key

A team lead's agent wraps one paid API; teammates' agents call it by name.
None of them ever sees the key, and one call revokes any of them.

1. Store the key once, encrypted, never returned by any tool:
   ```
   host.secret.set(name="stripe", value="sk_live_...")
   ```
2. Publish the wrapper. The header references the secret by name; the host
   interpolates it at call time, and callers' `tools/list` entry never
   shows a `secret.*` parameter:
   ```
   host.tool.publish(name="stripe_balance", kind="http", spec={
     "method": "GET", "url": "https://api.stripe.com/v1/balance",
     "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer {{ secret.stripe }}"}
   })
   ```
3. Create a group for the team:
   ```
   host.group.create(name="finance")
   ```
4. Share the tool to that group:
   ```
   host.tool.share(name="stripe_balance", visibility="group", group="finance")
   ```
5. Add each teammate's tenant by namespace:
   ```
   host.group.add(name="finance", namespace="<teammate_namespace>")
   ```
6. A teammate's agent calls it like any other tool -- no key, ever:
   ```
   host.tool.call(name="<owner_namespace>.stripe_balance", args={})
   ```

Revoke one teammate any time with `host.group.remove(name, namespace)` --
their next call fails, the rest keep working, no republish needed. Runnable
end-to-end proof: `examples/share-a-tool/proof.sh`.

### Share a tool, not a key: public variant

Step 4 can instead be `host.tool.share(name="stripe_balance",
visibility="public")` -- discoverable by anyone via `host.catalog.search`,
no group or step 5 needed. `group` is the default above because a tool
built around `{{ secret.<name> }}` almost always wraps a paid, rate-limited,
or ToS-restricted upstream account: `public` invites call volume from
strangers against that same account, with no allowlist standing between
them and your key's rate limit or bill. Reach for `public` when the tool
has no paid or limited upstream behind it -- a free API, or a tool with no
secrets at all.
<!-- sharing:end -->

### Share a tool, and let them read it

Step 4 above only lets a teammate *call* the tool. Pass `expose_spec: true`
on the same call to also let them read it -- the difference between handing
someone a paid API and letting them fork your code:
```
host.tool_share(name="stripe_balance", visibility="group", group="finance",
                 expose_spec=true)
```
A group member now reads the tool's kind and (redacted) spec with:
```
host.tool_spec_shared(tool="<owner_namespace>.stripe_balance")
-> {"tool": "<owner_namespace>.stripe_balance", "kind": "http",
    "spec": {"url": "...", "method": "GET"}, "exposed_at": "2026-09-26T..."}
```
`env`, `secrets`, and any `{{ secret.<name> }}` reference never appear in
that response, regardless of `expose_spec` -- the owner's key stays exactly
as hidden as it was under "Share a tool, not a key" above. Default is
`expose_spec: false`: an already-shared tool stays call-only until the
owner opts in. Reading it counts against the reader's own call quota, same
as `host.tool_call` does -- no separate quota to track. Shared without the
flag, `host.tool_spec_shared` fails with `spec_not_exposed`; not shared at
all, it fails exactly like `host.tool_call` does on an unshared tool --
`tool_not_found`, never revealing whether the tool exists.

<!-- recipe:team-memory begin -->
## Recipe calls: Give your agents one memory

The exact calls, in order (generated from `recipes/team-memory.toml`; do not hand-edit -- run `cargo xtask recipes`). Plan fit: free.

Sign up first (`signup`), once per tenant: `owner`, `teammate`.

1. `host.table.create(columns={"at":"real","key":"text","tags":"json","text":"text","writer":"text"}, name="memory")` [owner]
2. `host.tool_publish(kind="python", name="remember", spec={"source":"<contents of examples/team-memory/tools/remember.py>"})` [owner]
3. `host.tool_publish(kind="python", name="recall", spec={"source":"<contents of examples/team-memory/tools/recall.py>"})` [owner]
4. `host.group.create(name="team")` [owner]
5. `host.tool_share(group="team", name="remember", visibility="group")` [owner]
6. `host.tool_share(group="team", name="recall", visibility="group")` [owner]
7. `host.group.add(name="team", namespace="<teammate_namespace>")` [owner]
8. `host.tool_call(args={"key":"deploy","text":"deploy window is Tuesday 9pm","who":"<teammate_namespace>"}, name="<owner_namespace>.remember")` [teammate] -- writer holds the caller's own namespace
9. `host.tool_call(args={"query":"deploy"}, name="<owner_namespace>.recall")` [teammate]
   expect `$.rows[0].key` = "deploy"

Expected cost: 11 calls (the 2 signups included), within 90 s.
<!-- recipe:team-memory end -->

## Give your agents one memory

A team's agents write to and search one shared log instead of each keeping
its own. Every row remembers who wrote it.

1. Create the table once, on the owner's tenant:
   ```
   host.table.create(name="memory", columns={
     "key": "text", "text": "text", "tags": "json",
     "writer": "text", "at": "real"
   })
   ```
2. Publish the two tools (`python` kind, source omitted below for space --
   `writer` holds the caller's tenant namespace, `at` an epoch timestamp):
   ```
   host.tool_publish(name="remember", kind="python", spec={"source": "..."})
   host.tool_publish(name="recall", kind="python", spec={"source": "..."})
   ```
   mcphost does not yet expose a caller's own tenant id inside a shared
   `python` tool (open question, this recipe's own load-bearing check), so
   `remember` takes a `who` argument and trusts it: state your own tenant
   namespace when you call it. That is what `writer` holds today; the day
   the host exposes the real caller id to a shared tool, `who` becomes
   optional and `writer` stops trusting it.
3. Create a group for the team:
   ```
   host.group.create(name="team")
   ```
4. Share both tools to it:
   ```
   host.tool_share(name="remember", visibility="group", group="team")
   host.tool_share(name="recall", visibility="group", group="team")
   ```
5. Add each teammate's tenant by namespace:
   ```
   host.group.add(name="team", namespace="<teammate_namespace>")
   ```
6. Any teammate remembers and recalls like any shared tool:
   ```
   host.tool_call(name="<owner_namespace>.remember", args={
     "key": "deploy", "text": "deploy window is Tuesday 9pm",
     "who": "<my_own_namespace>"})
   host.tool_call(name="<owner_namespace>.recall", args={"query": "deploy"})
   ```

`recall` matches key/text/tags by substring, newest first, capped at 50
rows even if you ask for more. The table is the owner's: shared tools run
in the owner's tenant (`src/sharing.rs`), so rows count against the
owner's `table_rows_max`/`table_bytes_max`, and
`host.group.remove(name, namespace)` cuts a teammate off on their next
call, no republish needed. Runnable end-to-end proof:
`examples/team-memory/proof.sh`.

<!-- idempotency:start -->
## Idempotency

Any `tools/call` may carry `_meta.idempotency_key` (or `args.__idempotency_key` for clients that drop `_meta`); the host stores the first result for 24 h and a repeat with the same key and args returns it with `_meta.replayed: true` without running the tool. The same key with different args answers `idempotency_conflict` (use a new key for a different request). A `tool_timeout` error says: retry with the same _meta.idempotency_key to get the stored result.
<!-- idempotency:end -->

<!-- notify:start -->
## Notify your user

Register where your user lives once with `host.notify.channel_add {kind, target}` (kind is one of `email`, `webhook`, `slack`), then reach them with `host.notify.send {text, level, link?}` (level is one of `info`, `warn`, `action`); `host.notify.receipts` shows per-channel delivery. An unknown kind answers `notify_kind_unknown` (`/help/notify_kind_unknown`).
<!-- notify:end -->

## Limits and pricing

- 50 tools per tenant; tool names match `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{1,40}$`
- Spec at most 64 KiB; request body at most 1 MiB; a **synchronous** tool output at most 1 MiB (over either returns a structured error naming the cap and the size received, never a bare parse failure) -- an **async** job's own result has no such cap, see "Long-running jobs" below
- Call timeout: 30 s by default, or your own `timeout_s` up to 60 s max -- declare it and the host holds to it, not a hidden shorter deadline
- Concurrent calls: 20 concurrent calls host-wide; per tenant, 4 per tenant on the free plan (10 on pro) -- a refusal past your own cap is `concurrency_exceeded`/`scope: "tenant"` with `in_flight`, `limit` and `retry_after_ms`; past the host cap it's `scope: "host"`
- Keys are 32-byte random bearer tokens, stored as SHA-256 hashes
- Free plan (early access, default at signup): 500 calls per day, no card required
- Pro plan: $19/month, 50,000 calls per month included, then $0.001 per call
- A tool that needs more than the call deadline runs as a job instead:
  `host.tool_call(name, args, async=true)` returns `{run_id, status: "queued"}`
  within ~50 ms; the job runs under the plan's `job_max_s` deadline (free
  300 s, pro 900 s), up to `jobs_concurrent` at once per tenant (free 1, pro
  3), reporting progress and a result through `host.runs.get`/`list`/
  `cancel`/`purge`/`wait`. `host.usage`'s `jobs` block and `host.quickstart`'s
  `limits.plan` both report the same two numbers. A big result, structured
  counters, and the quota/retention story for both: see "Long-running jobs"
  below.
- Machine-readable catalog, the same numbers `billing.plans` returns:
  [`/plans.json`](/plans.json), rendered at [`/plans.html`](/plans.html) and
  `docs/plans.md`.

## Long-running jobs

The sync cap above, the async job flow, structured progress, and retention
all in one place -- the two were documented separately before this section
existed, so an agent found out about the cap only after a five-minute job
finished.

- **Sync cap, unchanged:** a synchronous call's own output over
  `MAX_TOOL_OUTPUT_BYTES` (1 MiB) fails `tool_output_too_large` (`python`
  kind) or `response_too_large` (`http` kind), naming the limit and the
  size received -- exactly as today, whether the tool ran async before or
  not.
- **Async results never fail for size:** an async job's result over 1 MiB
  is chunked into 256 KiB parts and stored in your tenant's own state, not
  rejected. `host.runs.get`/`host.runs.wait` inline part 0 as `result` and
  report `result_ref: {parts, bytes, content_type}`; read any part
  (including the tail) with `host.runs.part(run_id, n)` -- a result that
  fit inline reads back `parts: 1, n: 0` with the whole result, so there's
  one read path either way.
- **Structured counters:** `host.progress(run_id, counters={"items_processed":
  n, "items_total"?: n, "bytes_out"?: n, "custom"?: {...}})` reports a
  count readable mid-run (not just at the end) via `host.runs.get`/`wait`/
  `list`'s `counters` field -- each counter is monotonic on its own, a
  lower value than what's already stored fails `validation` with nothing
  written. `host.runs.wait(run_id, until={"counter": "items_processed",
  "gte": n})` returns as soon as that counter reaches `n`, or the run
  finishes, whichever comes first.
- **Quota, not silent truncation:** if storing the parts would exceed your
  plan's `state_bytes_max`, no part is written and the run finalizes
  `status: "error", error: {kind: "state_quota", data: {needed_bytes,
  available_bytes}}` -- counters reported before the failure are still
  there.
- **Retention:** `host.runs.purge(before_unix)` deletes a done run's parts
  the same way it always cleared a plain result; `host.usage`'s
  `run_results_bytes` reports how much of your state quota run parts hold,
  separately from your own `host.state.*` writes.

Walk-through (the tool itself omitted for space -- any python tool that
calls `progress`/returns a large result works; substitute your own
`<run_id>` for the one `host.tool_call` returns):

```
host.tool_publish(name="bulk_enrich", kind="python", spec={"source": "..."})
host.tool_call(name="bulk_enrich", args={"n": 1468006}, async=true)
host.progress(run_id="<run_id>", counters={"items_processed": 1000})
host.runs.wait(run_id="<run_id>")
host.runs.part(run_id="<run_id>", n=5)
```
  `limits.plan` both report the same two numbers.
- Every run row names the end user it ran as, when any: `host.runs.get`/
  `list`/`wait` carry `end_user: {subject, issuer, method} | null`.
  `host.runs.list(end_user_subject="...")` filters to just that end user's
  runs.

<!-- recipe:database-in-a-minute begin -->
## Recipe calls: Give Claude a database in one minute

The exact calls, in order (generated from `recipes/database-in-a-minute.toml`; do not hand-edit -- run `cargo xtask recipes`). Plan fit: free.

Sign up first (`signup`), once per tenant: `owner`.

1. `host.table.create(columns={"amount":"real","category":"text","day":"integer","id":"integer"}, name="expenses", primary_key="id")`
2. `host.table.append(rows=[{"amount":11.1,"category":"produce","day":1,"id":1},{"amount":7.25,"category":"produce","day":2,"id":2},{"amount":900.0,"category":"rent","day":3,"id":3},{"amount":32.5,"category":"transit","day":4,"id":4}], table="expenses")`
   expect `$.appended` = 4
3. `host.table.model_set(key="description", table="expenses", value="Household spending, one row per purchase.")`
4. `host.table.query(sql="SELECT category, SUM(amount) AS total FROM expenses GROUP BY category ORDER BY category")`
   expect `$.rows[0].category` = "produce"
5. `host.table.query(sql="SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM expenses WHERE category LIKE '%prod%'")`
   expect `$.rows[0].n` = 2
6. `host.table.query_log(limit=10)` -- the last calls newest first, each with its sql and row_count
   expect `$.rows[0].row_count` = 1

Expected cost: 7 calls (the 1 signup included), within 60 s.
<!-- recipe:database-in-a-minute end -->

## Give Claude a database in one minute

A CSV becomes a table your own Claude Desktop can query -- in plain SQL,
no query grammar to learn, no tool to publish. No server, no Airtable
account. Free-plan fit: 1 table, up to 1,000 rows of the 5,000-row
`table_rows_max` quota, append batches sized to stay under
`table_bytes_max`.

1. One call, no file tool needed -- the server fetches the 1,000-row fixture itself:
   ```
   host.table.create(name="expenses", source_url="https://mcphost.dev/examples/sample-1000.csv")
   ```
2. Or declare the table yourself (typed columns: text, integer, real, timestamp,
   boolean, json) and append your rows in batches of 200 -- five calls covers 1,000 rows:
   ```
   host.table.create(name="expenses", columns={
     "id": "integer", "category": "text", "amount": "real", "day": "integer"
   }, primary_key="id")
   host.table.append(table="expenses", rows=[
     {"id": 1, "category": "produce", "amount": 11.10, "day": 1}, ...
   ])
   ```
3. Leave a note so any agent reading the schema knows what a column means:
   ```
   host.table.model_set(table="expenses", key="description",
     value="Household spending, one row per purchase.")
   ```
4. Ask questions straight in SQL -- CTEs, GROUP BY, LIKE, all of it:
   ```
   host.table.query(sql="SELECT category, SUM(amount) AS total \
     FROM expenses GROUP BY category")
   host.table.query(sql="SELECT * FROM expenses WHERE category LIKE '%prod%'")
   ```
5. Review what was asked: `host.table.query_log(limit=10)` lists the last
   calls newest first, each with its `sql`, `row_count` (or a refusal's
   `error_code`), and `duration_ms`.
6. Connect Claude Desktop: add the tenant's endpoint and bearer key as an
   MCP server in `claude_desktop_config.json`:
   ```
   {"mcpServers": {"my-data": {"url": "<endpoint>/mcp",
     "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer <key>"}}}}
   ```

Writing your own `python` tool against this same table instead?
`mcphost.table.query(sql)` is the bridge to it -- `mcphost.state.query`
reaches the separate key-value store, not this one.

Runnable end-to-end proof, 1,000-row fixture included:
`examples/database-in-a-minute/proof.sh`.

<!-- recipe:chart-in-a-minute begin -->
## Recipe calls: Chart in a minute

The exact calls, in order (generated from `recipes/chart-in-a-minute.toml`; do not hand-edit -- run `cargo xtask recipes`). Plan fit: free.

Sign up first (`signup`), once per tenant: `owner`.

1. `host.table.create(columns={"amount":"real","category":"text","day":"integer","id":"integer"}, name="expenses", primary_key="id")`
2. `host.table.append(rows=[{"amount":11.1,"category":"produce","day":1,"id":1},{"amount":7.25,"category":"produce","day":2,"id":2},{"amount":900.0,"category":"rent","day":3,"id":3},{"amount":32.5,"category":"transit","day":4,"id":4}], table="expenses")`
   expect `$.appended` = 4
3. `host.table.chart(share=true, sql="SELECT category, SUM(amount) AS total FROM expenses GROUP BY category")` -- the mark is picked from the columns' types; share_url opens with no login
   expect `$.schema` = "chart.v1"
   expect `$.share_url` is present
   expect `$.vega_lite` is present

Expected cost: 4 calls (the 1 signup included), within 60 s.
<!-- recipe:chart-in-a-minute end -->

## Chart in a minute

One SQL call turns a question into a chart spec, a data-computed caption,
and a link -- no chart grammar, you name the data with `sql`.

1. Reuse the `expenses` table, through `host.table.*` (the real-SQL store
   `host.table.query` already reads, not `host.state.*` above):
   ```
   host.table.create(name="expenses", columns={
     "id": "integer", "category": "text", "amount": "real", "day": "integer"
   })
   host.table.append(table="expenses", rows=[
     {"id": 1, "category": "produce", "amount": 11.10, "day": 1}, ...
   ])
   ```
2. Ask for the picture:
   ```
   host.table.chart(
     sql="SELECT category, SUM(amount) AS total FROM expenses GROUP BY category",
     share=true)
   ```
   Returns `{schema: "chart.v1", profile, recommendation: {mark, encoding,
   rationale, alternatives}, vega_lite, caption: {headline, facts},
   share_url}`. The mark is picked from the columns' types, not guessed by
   a model; every caption number is recomputed from the rows that came
   back.
3. Paste `share_url` to a teammate -- it opens with no login, for 24 hours:
   ```
   https://<host>/charts/<id>?exp=<unix>&sig=<hex>
   ```

Runnable end-to-end proof, 1,000-row fixture included:
`examples/chart-in-a-minute/proof.sh`.

<!-- recipe:webhook-inbox begin -->
## Recipe calls: Webhook inbox in one call

The exact calls, in order (generated from `recipes/webhook-inbox.toml`; do not hand-edit -- run `cargo xtask recipes`). Plan fit: free.

Sign up first (`signup`), once per tenant: `owner`.

1. `host.webhook_inbox.create(name="inbox")` -- returns url, secret and wait in one call
   expect `$.url` contains "/hook/"
   expect `$.secret` is present
   expect `$.wait.tool` = "host.msg.wait"
2. POST `{"id":"evt-fixture-1"}` to `<step1.url>`, signed (HMAC-SHA256 under the secret, `X-Mcphost-Signature: sha256=<hex>`), expect HTTP 200 -- a signed POST, exactly as a sender would
3. POST `{"id":"evt-fixture-1"}` to `<step1.url>`, unsigned, expect HTTP 401 -- an unsigned POST is refused and stores nothing
4. `host.tool_call(args={}, name="inbox")` -- the last 50 stored events as rows
   expect `$.rows[0].id` = "evt-fixture-1"
5. `host.msg.wait()` -- pass wait.args from step 1 as-is
   expect `$.messages[0].data.event_id` = "evt-fixture-1"

Expected cost: 4 calls (the 1 signup included), within 90 s.
<!-- recipe:webhook-inbox end -->

## Webhook inbox in one call

An agent that must show its user a webhook arriving needs a public URL and a
way to read the next event, without writing a server. One call creates both.

1. Create the inbox (works on the free plan):
   ```
   host.webhook_inbox.create(name="inbox")
   ```
   Returns `{url, secret, tool: "inbox", trigger_id, wait: {tool: "host.msg.wait", args}, next}`.
   `url` is `https://<host>/hook/<id>`; `secret` is shown once. Calling it
   again with the same `name` returns the same `url` and no `secret`
   (`rotate: true` mints a new one). `verify` is `hmac` (default), `github` or
   `stripe`. A tenant at its plan's trigger ceiling gets `plan_limit` with
   `data.limit`, and nothing is created.
2. Point the sender at `url` and sign the raw body with HMAC-SHA256 under
   `secret`: `X-Mcphost-Signature: sha256=<hex>` (GitHub: `X-Hub-Signature-256`).
   An unsigned or wrongly signed POST is `401` and stores nothing.
3. Read the event, either way:
   ```
   host.tool_call(name="inbox")
   host.msg.wait(timeout_s=25, unread_only=true)
   ```
   The first returns the last 50 stored events as `rows` (`id` is the body's
   own `id`); the second blocks until a delivery arrives and returns a
   message from `@host` whose `data.event_id` names it. Pass `wait.args`
   from step 1 as-is.

`host.msg.wait` and `host.runs.wait` block for at most 25 s (`limits.wait_max_s` in `host.quickstart`; default 20 s). A wait that ends with nothing to report returns `timed_out: true`, `waited_ms` and `timeout_s_applied`: call again.

/mcp keeps no state between requests: pass `tenant_key` on every call, or
reconnect over your `/u/` URL. A key-less call right after `host.redeem` is
refused with `tenant_key_missing` naming your tenant, never a second tenant.

Runnable end-to-end proof: `examples/webhook-inbox/proof.sh`.

## Audit what your key did

`host.calls.list {since: "-24h", key_label?, tool?, outcome?, credential?, limit, cursor}` returns every
call made with your keys, newest first: `ts`, `credential` (`primary`, `sub_key`, `oauth`, `trigger`,
`cron`, `webhook`, `shared_caller`), `key_label` for a sub-key's rows, `tool`, `outcome`, `duration_ms`,
`bytes_in`, `bytes_out`. A sub-key sees only its own rows. A window older than your plan's
`calls_retention_days` (`host.quickstart` `limits.plan`; Free 7, Pro 90) comes back with
`truncated_before`.

`host.calls.export {since, until}` returns the same rows as `csv` plus `rows`, `sha256`, an ES256
`signature` over the CSV bytes, and the `kid` of the key in `/.well-known/jwks.json` that verifies it
(over 50 000 rows is `too_many_rows`: narrow the window). Verify without an mcphost account:

```
# save csv to calls.csv and signature_der (base64) to sig.b64, then:
base64 -d sig.b64 > sig.bin
# turn the JWK with that kid into jwks-key.pem (EC P-256, x and y), then:
openssl dgst -sha256 -verify jwks-key.pem -signature sig.bin calls.csv
```

## Billing (tool calls, no dashboard)

- `billing.plans()`: the plan catalog and `billing_mode` (`test` or `live`). Works anonymously.
- `billing.status()`: this tenant's plan and usage against each quota, with `resets_at` for the daily call quota.
- `billing.checkout(plan="pro")`: returns a Stripe Checkout `url` (valid about 24 hours). Hand it to the human who authorized you; when they pay, a webhook flips the tenant to `pro` within seconds. Call `billing.status` to confirm.
- A call past a quota fails with `error_code: quota_exceeded`, `plan`, `limit {name, value}`, `used`, and `next: "billing.checkout"`. Do not retry; upgrade or wait for `resets_at`.

## Measured performance

- 200 concurrent `echo` calls: p95 34.20 ms, 0 errors, 37.3 MiB RSS (acceptance test AC11, Hetzner CPX21-class box) <!-- cite: docs/benchmarks/ac11-load-smoke.txt -->
- Published tools appear in `tools/list` immediately; no cache layer

## Operator notes

- Admin runs through `admin.*` tools on the same endpoint with an admin key; there is no web UI by design.
- Per-tenant metering (p50/p95 durations, call counts) via `host.usage` and `admin.usage`.
- An old `plans.toml` missing a quota (e.g. one written before `state_bytes_max` existed) is filled from `default_catalog()`'s value for that plan name, never zeroed; startup logs `plans.toml: plan=<name> defaulted=[<field>, ...]` naming exactly what it filled in.
- OAuth conformance: `mcphost oauth-probe --url <mcp-url> --json` runs the same scenario table the gate runs in-process; every scenario, its family, owning PRD and expected verdict are listed in [docs/oauth-scenarios.md](../docs/oauth-scenarios.md).
- `oauth.tenants_7d.issuer_jwt + oauth.tenants_7d.hosted_token` on `admin healthz` (distinct non-synthetic tenants, both credential kinds) is the `oauth_tenants_7d` loop metric, documented in [docs/metrics.md](../docs/metrics.md) -- `admin.oauth.demand_stats` has the same counts plus the per-tenant breakdown and the registration/consent/token funnel.
- `scripts/oauth-conformance.sh <mcp-url>` runs the MCP OAuth conformance suite (`npx @modelcontextprotocol/conformance`, scenarios `auth/basic-metadata-var1` and `auth/basic-dcr`, requirements `2026-07-28`) against a running host and writes `docs/receipts/oauth-conformance-<date>.md`; exits non-zero on any failed scenario, or `2` with a one-line reason when `npx` isn't installed.
- `help_url_served` on `admin healthz` -- a `{code: count}` object of how many times each `/help/<code>` page has been served since this process started, documented in [docs/metrics.md](../docs/metrics.md); `/status.json`'s readiness carries a warning when `MCPHOST_SUPPORT_URL` is unset, never a silent blank.

<!-- capabilities:start -->
## Capabilities

Generated by `mcphost capabilities-section` from the `CAPABILITIES` registry -- the same rows `initialize.capabilities` and `GET /capabilities.json` are built from; do not hand-edit. A method of a primitive marked `no` answers `-32601` with `data.help_url` (`/help/capability_unsupported`) and `data.alternative`. `server_to_client` lists the methods the host SENDS rather than receives: a client posting one gets `-32601` with `data.code = method_server_to_client`.

| primitive | implemented | list_changed | probe | alternative | methods | server_to_client |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `tools` | yes | yes | `tools` | - | `tools/list`, `tools/call` | - |
| `resources` | yes | no | `resources` | `host.table.list` | `resources/list`, `resources/read`, `resources/templates/list`, `resources/subscribe`, `resources/unsubscribe` | - |
| `prompts` | yes | yes | `prompts` | `host.quickstart` | `prompts/list`, `prompts/get` | - |
| `completions` | no | no | `completions` | `host.help.search` | `completion/complete` | - |
| `sampling` | yes | no | `sampling` | - | `sampling/createMessage` | `sampling/createMessage` |
| `elicitation` | yes | no | `elicitation` | `host.ask.create` | `elicitation/create` | `elicitation/create` |
| `logging` | no | no | `logging` | - | `logging/setLevel` | - |
| `roots` | no | no | `roots` | - | `roots/list` | `roots/list` |
<!-- capabilities:end -->

<!-- frames:start -->
## Transport

Generated by `scripts/protocol-frames-check.sh` from `FRAME_SEQUENCES`; do not hand-edit. A response is `application/json` when it is one frame and `text/event-stream` when more than one frame is sent (`{1}` exactly one, `{0,1}` optional, `{0,n}` any number). Take the last `result` or `error` frame. Per request type, in order: `initialize` = `result` {1}; `tools/list` = `result` {1}; `tools/call:keyed` = `notifications/tools/list_changed` {0,1}, `notifications/prompts/list_changed` {0,1}, `result` {1}; `tools/call:keyless_signup` = `notifications/tools/list_changed` {0,1}, `result` {1}; `tools/call:error` = `error` {1}; `tools/call:with_progress_token` = `notifications/progress` {0,n}, `result` {1} (when request _meta.progressToken present); `ping` = `error` {1}. Every `/mcp` response carries `Server-Timing: app;dur=<ms>`: the host's wall time from the request reaching the route (auth and rate-limit time included) to the response head being ready, so a `text/event-stream` response reports time to response head, not to its last frame. Caddy, TLS and network time are not included. Machine-readable: [/protocol/frames.json](/protocol/frames.json).
<!-- frames:end -->

## Contract

The `host.*`/`billing.*` tool surface below is a versioned, committed contract: [contracts/host-tools.v1.json](../contracts/host-tools.v1.json) (`host.whoami`'s `contract_version`). Removing or narrowing a field fails the build unless it was announced first (`x-deprecated` on the affected tool/field in `tools/list`, a `deprecations` note on any call that uses it) with at least 60 days' notice. Call `host.changelog({since})` for what's changed since a given release.

## Paging

These verbs take `limit` and `cursor` and offer an `order` (pass `next_cursor` back with the same `order`; a cursor minted under another order is `cursor_invalid`):

- host.channel.read: orders `seq_asc`; default `seq_asc`.
- host.msg.inbox: orders `created_asc`; default `created_asc`.
- host.msg.thread: orders `seq_asc`; default `seq_asc`.
- host.runs.list: orders `created_desc`, `created_asc`; default `created_desc`.
- host.calls.list: orders `newest_first`; default `newest_first`.
- host.docs.list: orders `created_desc`, `created_asc`, `name_asc`; default `created_desc`.

## Indexes

- host.index.create sources[].kind is one of: doc, table, url.
<!-- tools:end -->
<!-- events:start -->
## Events

Generated by `mcphost llms-txt` from `src/events.rs` -- the same list `GET /events.json` serves; do not hand-edit.

- run.done — A tool run finished successfully; data: run_id, tool, status, duration_ms
- run.failed — A tool run ended in an error; data: run_id, tool, status, error_code
- run.progress — A running tool wrote a progress update; data: run_id, tool, progress
- inbox.message — A message arrived in the tenant's inbox; data: message_id, channel, from
- table.changed — A row was appended to, updated in or deleted from a table; data: table, op, row_id
- state.changed — A state key was set or deleted; data: key, op
- queue.drained — A queue went empty after being non-empty; data: queue
- queue.dead_letter — A queue item exhausted its attempts and moved to dead letters; data: queue, item_id, attempts
- trigger.fired — A trigger fired; data.trigger_kind says which sort; data: trigger_id, trigger_kind
- tool.published — A tool was published or republished; data: tool, version
<!-- events:end -->

## REST façade

No MCP client? Every plain-HTTP route is described by OpenAPI 3.1 at `/openapi.json` and rendered at `/docs`.

## Retry policy

Generated by `mcphost retry-policy` from `RETRY_POLICY` -- the same rows every error's `data.retry {retryable, after_ms, attempts_left, policy}` is built from; do not hand-edit. Sleep `after_ms` before a retry; send `_meta.attempt` so `attempts_left` counts down. Machine-readable: `/retry_policy.json`.

| code | retryable | backoff | max attempts | policy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bearer_invalid` | no | none | 1 | reauthenticate |
| `tenant_key_missing` | no | none | 1 | fix-and-resend |
| `tenant_key_invalid` | no | none | 1 | reauthenticate |
| `forbidden` | no | none | 1 | do-not-retry |
| `tenant_disabled` | no | none | 1 | do-not-retry |
| `rate_limited` | yes | exponential(1000ms, max 30000ms) | 3 | honour-retry-after |
| `tool_not_found` | no | none | 1 | do-not-retry |
| `tenant_not_found` | no | none | 1 | do-not-retry |
| `invalid_params` | no | none | 1 | fix-and-resend |
| `unknown_kind` | no | none | 1 | fix-and-resend |
| `invalid_tool_name` | no | none | 1 | fix-and-resend |
| `spec_too_large` | no | none | 1 | fix-and-resend |

## Upstream connections

Generated by `mcphost gen-docs` from `providers.toml` -- do not hand-edit. Call `host.connect.providers` to see which providers this host can connect right now (`available`, and `reason` when not) and the exact scope names each accepts; the full tables are in docs/connections.md.

- `github` -- refresh `none`, 5 scope(s)
- `google` -- refresh `offline_access`, 6 scope(s)
- `notion` -- refresh `none`, 0 scope(s)
- `slack` -- refresh `rotating`, 5 scope(s)
<!-- connections:end -->

<!-- recipe:data-sync begin -->
## Recipe calls: Data sync: mirror a CSV into a table

The exact calls, in order (generated from `recipes/data-sync.toml`; do not hand-edit -- run `cargo xtask recipes`). Plan fit: free.

Sign up first (`signup`), once per tenant: `owner`.

1. `host.sync.create(source=<a csv-over-http source, ref = the public url of your CSV>, table="orders", mode="pull")` -- registers the source and creates the `orders` table; the host does not fetch at create time
   expect `$.sync_id` is present
   expect `$.next_run_unix` is present
   expect `$.status` is present
   expect `$.table` = "orders"
   expect `$.existing` = false
2. `host.sync.run_now(sync_id="<step1.sync_id>")` -- makes the sync due now; the trigger tick picks it up
   expect `$.next_run_unix` is present
3. `host.sync.get(sync_id="<step1.sync_id>")` -- the sync row; polled until the first receipt (`last_run`) exists: `ok`, 12 rows added, change detected
   expect `$.table` = "orders"
   expect `$.last_run.run_id` is present
   expect `$.last_run.started_unix` is present
   expect `$.last_run.status` = "ok"
   expect `$.last_run.change_detected` = true
   expect `$.last_run.rows_added` = 12
4. `host.sync.run_now(sync_id="<step1.sync_id>")` -- makes the sync due again; the CSV has not changed
   expect `$.next_run_unix` is present
5. `host.sync.get(sync_id="<step1.sync_id>")` -- polled until the second receipt exists: `ok`, no change detected, 0 rows added
   expect `$.table` = "orders"
   expect `$.last_run.status` = "ok"
   expect `$.last_run.change_detected` = false
   expect `$.last_run.rows_added` = 0
6. `host.sync.list()`
   expect `$.syncs[0].table` = "orders"
7. `host.sync.delete(sync_id="<step1.sync_id>")` -- stops the schedule; the `orders` table stays
   expect `$.deleted` = true
   expect `$.table_kept` = true

Expected cost: 8 calls (the 1 signup included), within 95 s.
<!-- recipe:data-sync end -->

<!-- sync:start -->
## Data sync

Generated by `mcphost gen-docs` from `src/sync/mod.rs` -- do not hand-edit. `host.sync.create` mirrors an external dataset into a host table on a schedule (`every`, default `*/15 * * * *`, never faster than 300 s); a free tenant holds `syncs_max` of them (`host.quickstart` `limits.plan`). `source.kind` is one of:

- `csv_url` -- ref is a public http(s) URL of a CSV file; no connection needed
- `google_sheet` -- ref is a spreadsheet id, or the sheet's URL; needs a connected account (host.connect.start)
- `airtable` -- ref is a base id and table id joined by a slash, appXXXX/tblXXXX; needs a connected account (host.connect.start)
- `notion_db` -- ref is a database id; needs a connected account (host.connect.start)
- `http_json` -- ref is a public http(s) URL answering a JSON array of objects; no connection needed
<!-- sync:end -->

  (echo, http, python, wasm, chain), all measured benchmarks, and supporting
  receipts, concatenated into one markdown file per the llms.txt convention.

## Recipe calls: Uptime probes with no server

The exact calls, in order (generated from `recipes/uptime-probes.toml`; do not hand-edit -- run `cargo xtask recipes`). Plan fit: free.

Sign up first (`signup`), once per tenant: `owner`.

1. `host.uptime.create(name="status", urls=["<fixture_base>/health","<fixture_base>/health?second=1"])` -- creates the probe set, a status tool and one schedule, and probes once
   expect `$.status_tool` = "status"
   expect `$.schedule_id` is present
   expect `$.first_result.rows[0].ok` = true
2. `host.tool_call(args={}, name="status")` -- reads the last stored result, never fetches live

Expected cost: 3 calls (the 1 signup included), within 60 s.
<!-- recipe:uptime-probes end -->

## Uptime probes with no server

An agent that runs its own small services wants to know when one is down,
without a monitoring SaaS account, a server of its own, or a plan upgrade.
One call; the host does the probing, so no sandbox network is involved.

1. Create the probe set (works on the free plan):
   ```
   host.uptime.create(name="status", urls=["https://api.example.com/health", "https://example.com"])
   ```
   Takes 1 to 20 URLs and creates the `status_targets` table, a host-side
   probe (3 s per URL, same host rules as the `http` kind), a `status` tool
   and one schedule. It runs the probe once before answering:
   `{status_tool, schedule_id, every_s, next_fire_unix, first_result: {columns, rows, text}}`.
   An `every_s` below your plan's floor is raised to it and the response
   carries `data.clamped_to`.
2. Show the table any time -- reads the last stored result, never fetches live:
   ```
   host.tool_call(name="status")
   ```
   returns `{columns, rows, text}`; `text` is an aligned table under 2 KB to
   paste to your user. A target that did not answer in 3 s is `status: "timeout"`.

Plan numbers (generated from `src/plans.rs` by `mcphost llms-txt`; do not hand-edit):
- free: <!-- uprg:free.schedules_max -->3<!-- /uprg:free.schedules_max --> schedules, a floor of <!-- uprg:free.schedule_min_interval_s -->300<!-- /uprg:free.schedule_min_interval_s --> s between probes, so <!-- uprg:free.calls_per_day_at_floor -->288<!-- /uprg:free.calls_per_day_at_floor --> probe calls a day at the floor.
- pro: <!-- uprg:pro.schedules_max -->25<!-- /uprg:pro.schedules_max --> schedules, a floor of <!-- uprg:pro.schedule_min_interval_s -->60<!-- /uprg:pro.schedule_min_interval_s --> s, <!-- uprg:pro.calls_per_day_at_floor -->1440<!-- /uprg:pro.calls_per_day_at_floor --> probe calls a day at the floor.

Asking `host.tool_publish` for a python tool with `network: "public"` on the
free plan is refused with `data.alternative: "host.uptime.create"`.
